description: Hi! I'm building solo, from Singapore. I'm an engineering student and a trained singer with ten years of dance training, and I’ve recently started learning about music production.
summary: nāda turns two NASA Scientific Visualization Studio videos of Earth at night into music. A Python script measures every frame for lightning activity, surges, storm position, city glow and light gained or lost, and each measurement drives a musical decision at a fixed threshold. I produced the result in Logic Pro as two R&B tracks, and the website remixes the stems live from the same data, with written descriptions for visually impaired and low-vision listeners.
details:
Tools: Python (numpy, pandas, pretty_midi, ffmpeg), Logic Pro, HTML/CSS/JavaScript with the Web Audio API, GitHub Pages.
Code: https://github.com/sharvaripb/nada

What it does: nāda turns two NASA Scientific Visualization Studio videos of the Earth at night into music, lightning recorded from the ISS between 2017 and 2023, and Black Marble city lights between 2012 and 2023. A Python script measures every frame (around 7,800 in total), which gives us information about how much lightning is visible, sudden surges, where the storms are, city glow, and light gained or lost in four regions. Each measurement triggers one musical decision once it crosses a fixed threshold. A lightning surge 25% above its recent level becomes a drum roll, storms further north lift the vocal, cities that grew brighter lift the chords, and where light was lost, the drums fall silent.

How it’s creative: The data wrote the scores I used when I made the tracks. The measurements become MIDI, and with the help of Logic Pro, I wrote the chords, designed the sound, recorded my own vocals, and mixed and produced two R&B tracks. On the website, the stems keep mixing live from the same data while the NASA video plays, and a panel shows what the data is doing to the music at each moment.

Benefits and impact: Earth science is usually shared as images. nāda lets people hear how the planet changes, and written descriptions plus full keyboard and screen-reader support open it to blind and low-vision audiences. The same method could turn any satellite record, such as wildfires, sea ice or air quality, into music for classrooms and museums.

Factors considered: Everything is in G minor at 88.6 BPM, the tempo at which both videos fit the bar grid, so the data doesn't produce clashing notes. The measurements are relative to each video instead of absolute counts, and the lightning globe rotates while it plays. Both these limits are stated on the site
dataRefs: Lightning Events Detected from the International Space Station, 2017–2023 (NASA SVS 5011)
Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023 (NASA SVS 5313)
